name: AccessiBit
author: AccessiBit

sections.description:
Connect your AccessiBit account in one click to install the accessibility
widget and read your site’s accessibility results directly in your WordPress
admin. There is no key to copy: you approve the connection in AccessiBit and
come straight back here.

When you connect, AccessiBit scans your homepage once, free of charge, and the
plugin shows you the first few issues it found along with the total. To scan
the rest of your pages, and to see every issue with the detail behind it, run a
full audit in the AccessiBit dashboard.

Customize the widget’s look and tools, and write and publish your
accessibility statement, without leaving WordPress: AccessiBit → Widget and
AccessiBit → Statement are the same screens as in the AccessiBit dashboard.
Put the published statement on any page with the Accessibility statement
block or the [accessibit_statement] shortcode.

Full audits of more pages and your plan are managed in the AccessiBit
dashboard; the plugin links straight to the right page for this site, and shows
you the score of the latest full audit it finds.

The admin screens are in English, with Italian and Spanish translations
delivered by WordPress.org language packs.

External services

This plugin connects to AccessiBit services, as follows.

When you click Connect, your own browser goes to AccessiBit:
* app.accessibit.com — you are sent there to sign in and approve the connection. This site’s address travels in that link, so AccessiBit can show you which site you are connecting and send you back here afterwards. This is a page you open, not a request the plugin makes, and nothing happens until you click Connect.

Requests made from your WordPress admin, by the plugin itself:
* api.accessibit.com — immediately after you approve, this site asks AccessiBit to turn the one-time approval into a key for this site. This site’s address is sent with it, so AccessiBit can check the approval was for this site. The key is returned to your server and never passes through your browser.
* api.accessibit.com — to read scan summaries and your account details. The key is sent to authenticate, along with the plugin’s version; the target site is identified by its AccessiBit site ID. Your WordPress site address is not sent in these requests.
* api.accessibit.com — when you disconnect, or delete the plugin, this site asks AccessiBit to revoke the key. Only the key itself is sent.
* api.accessibit.com — when you open the Widget or Statement screen, to read and save the widget’s settings and your accessibility statement, to preview the statement, and to fetch a download link for it. These calls go from your server, which adds the key; your browser only talks to your own WordPress. What is sent is what you entered on those screens, including the names and contact address you write into the statement. Where the statement has no contact name or email address yet, the Statement screen fills them in with your WordPress display name and email address, and sends them with its preview as soon as the screen opens, before you have changed or saved anything. The target site is identified by its AccessiBit site ID. When you download the statement, your browser opens that link: a short-lived address of the file in AccessiBit’s storage at Amazon Web Services (amazonaws.com).
* api.accessibit.com — when a page holding the Accessibility statement block or the [accessibit_statement] shortcode is viewed and the plugin does not yet know of a published statement, your server asks AccessiBit for it, at most once every fifteen minutes, so a statement published from the AccessiBit dashboard appears without opening the Statement screen. The key is sent to authenticate; nothing about the visitor is sent.
* api.accessibit.com — immediately after you connect, the plugin asks AccessiBit to run one free accessibility scan of your homepage, and then reads the result to show it here. AccessiBit requests your homepage from its own servers, as any visitor would, using the address registered for this site in your AccessiBit account. This happens only after you click Connect, and only for a site address whose domain you have verified in AccessiBit. It is one scan per site address: reconnecting or reinstalling the plugin shows you the stored result rather than scanning again. If a scan fails, the Accessibility screen offers a Try again button, because a failure is not a result; it can be used a small number of times and not immediately after a failure. Nothing retries on its own.

Requests made from your own browser, on the Widget screen’s Tools tab:
* cdn.accessibit.com — the tab shows your homepage in a frame with the widget in preview mode, so your browser loads the widget script from AccessiBit’s CDN there, whether or not the widget is switched on. In preview mode the widget sends nothing to AccessiBit: it shows the settings on your screen, counts no page view and checks no licence.

Requests made from your visitors’ browsers, and only if you switch the widget on:
* cdn.accessibit.com — serves the accessibility widget script, and its published appearance settings, to your site’s front end.
* api.accessibit.com — the widget script contacts AccessiBit to check that your account licenses it, and to count usage. It sends your AccessiBit account name and your site’s domain, once when it loads and once per page a visitor views. No cookies are sent and no visitor is identified.
* api.accessibit.com — if a visitor opens the widget’s page-summary feature, the widget sends your site’s domain and the readable text of the page the visitor is on, so AccessiBit can summarise it. This happens only on that visitor’s request, never automatically.

Requests made from your visitors’ browsers, and only on a page where you placed the Accessibility statement block or the [accessibit_statement] shortcode, once the statement is published:
* api.accessibit.com — the visitor’s browser loads your published statement in a frame from AccessiBit, which picks the language from the browser’s preferred languages, and then from cdn.accessibit.com, where the published statement is stored. The frame is loaded with no referrer, so the address of your page is not sent. No visitor is identified.

Links the plugin shows you, which contact nothing until you click them:
* app.accessibit.com — the AccessiBit dashboard. The plugin’s screens link out to it to scan the rest of your site and buy a plan. These are ordinary links in your browser: no request is made and nothing is sent to AccessiBit unless you follow one.

The plugin’s own requests carry the WordPress locale of the administrator
reading the screen (for example it_IT). This is a language tag, not your site
address. Your site address travels only where it is listed above: in the
Connect link you follow, and in the request that redeems the approval. The scan
findings themselves come back in Italian, whatever that locale says, and the
plugin marks them up as Italian so a screen reader pronounces them correctly;
the WCAG reference beside each one is in English. The plugin’s own screens are
translated.

AccessiBit’s terms of service: https://www.accessibit.com/eula
AccessiBit’s privacy policy: https://www.accessibit.com/legal/privacy

Source code

The Widget and Statement screens are a compiled, minified script,
admin/bundle/accessibit-admin.js, with its stylesheet. Their complete source
code is in the plugin itself, in admin/bundle/source/: the bundle in each
release is built from that source, with the direct dependencies pinned in its
package.json to the versions the shipped bundle used. Their own dependencies
are resolved afresh, so a rebuild is equivalent rather than byte-identical. To
build it yourself, with Node.js 22 or later:

cd admin/bundle/source/packages/site-admin && npm install && npm run build:wp

admin/bundle/source/README.md describes the layout. The source is licensed

GPLv2 or later, like the rest of the plugin; the third-party packages compiled
into the script are listed, with their licences, in
admin/bundle/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt.
sections.installation:
You need an AccessiBit account with this site in it. If you don’t have one yet,
you can create the account, and add the site, while connecting.

  1. Install and activate the plugin.
  2. Go to AccessiBit → Setup in wp-admin.
  3. Click Connect to AccessiBit. AccessiBit opens in your browser, where you
    sign in (or create an account) and approve the connection for this site. You
    are then brought back to wp-admin, connected.
  4. AccessiBit then scans your homepage once, free of charge, and shows you what
    it found on AccessiBit → Accessibility.
  5. On that same screen, tick Show the accessibility widget to put the widget
    on your site.

Nothing leaves your site before you click Connect. If your site address is not
one of the sites on your AccessiBit account, the Setup screen says so, names the
address it compared, and links you to where the site is added; once it is,
Check again picks it up.

Scanning requires the site’s domain to be verified in your AccessiBit account.
Until it is, the Accessibility screen says so and links to the page where you
verify it.
sections.faq:
My WordPress is in a subdirectory. What gets scanned?

The address registered for the site in your AccessiBit account, which is a domain
rather than a path. So an install at example.com/blog is scanned at
example.com — the root of the domain, not the WordPress install. The same
applies to every site of a subdirectory multisite: they share one domain and
therefore one free scan. If your WordPress is not at the root of its domain, run
your scans from the AccessiBit dashboard, where you can give the exact pages.

How do I put my accessibility statement on my site?

Write it on AccessiBit → Statement and publish it. Then add the
Accessibility statement block to a page, or paste the
[accessibit_statement] shortcode into one. Each visitor sees the statement in
their own language (Italian, English or Spanish); to always show one language,
pick it in the block’s settings or write [accessibit_statement lang="it"].

To link the statement from a menu or the footer, add that page to the menu
(Appearance → Menus, or the Navigation block in the Site Editor). The Statement
screen also gives you the statement’s own address, if you prefer to link to it
directly.

The statement is hosted by AccessiBit and shown in a frame, so a change you
publish reaches your page without editing it again. Until it is published the
block shows nothing to visitors; a statement first published from the AccessiBit
dashboard appears within fifteen minutes, or at once after you open the
Statement screen. If a caching plugin stored the page while it was still empty,
clear that page from its cache.

If your plan stops including the statement, AccessiBit stops showing it, and the
frame on your page is left empty. Remove the block or the shortcode, or renew
the plan to bring the statement back.

Does the widget work with a caching or optimization plugin?

Yes. The widget tag carries the attributes that Autoptimize, LiteSpeed Cache, WP
Rocket and Cloudflare Rocket Loader read as “leave this file alone”, so
JavaScript aggregation, minification and delayed execution all skip it. Page
caching needs no exception at all, because the tag is part of the cached HTML.

If your optimization plugin uses some other mechanism, exclude
cdn.accessibit.com from its JavaScript combining and minification. The widget
has to stay a separate file: it reads which account it belongs to from its own
script tag, so once it is merged into a combined bundle it can no longer find
it, and the widget simply stops appearing — with nothing in the console to tell
you why.
sections.changelog:
1.0.1

  • Customize the widget from WordPress, on the new AccessiBit → Widget screen,
    and try it on your own homepage before saving: the Tools tab previews it with
    your unsaved changes.
  • Write, publish and download your accessibility statement from WordPress, on
    the new AccessiBit → Statement screen.
  • Show your statement on any page with the new Accessibility statement block
    or the [accessibit_statement] shortcode.
  • Connect to AccessiBit in one click — sign in and approve in AccessiBit, with
    no API key to copy. The key AccessiBit issues is valid for this site only.
  • Sites connected with an API key pasted into an earlier version need to press
    Reconnect on the Setup screen once before they can edit the widget or the
    statement here: that key covers your whole AccessiBit account, and can no
    longer change a site. Reconnecting does not revoke the old key; if nothing
    else uses it, revoke it on the API keys page in AccessiBit.
  • Disconnecting, or deleting the plugin, now revokes that key in AccessiBit
    instead of only forgetting it here. Disconnect says when a key could not be
    revoked, such as an API key pasted into an earlier version.
  • The source code of the Widget and Statement screens ships with the plugin, in
    admin/bundle/source/.

1.0.0

  • First release.
  • Connect a site to AccessiBit with an API key.
  • One free accessibility scan of your homepage when you connect, with a preview
    of the issues found.
  • Switch the accessibility widget on and off.
  • See the score of your site’s latest full audit, if it has one.
  • Links into the AccessiBit dashboard to customize the widget, write your
    accessibility statement, scan the rest of your site, and buy a plan.
  • Admin screens in English, Italian and Spanish.
